content_voiceover: This slide brings the full picture together for the propagation phase. The original extrinsic tenase complex on the upper left is now shown faded and gray, reflecting that TFPI has shut it down and it's no longer the main driver. Instead, the action has shifted to the right and bottom of the diagram, where factor eight, entering from outside, has been activated to eight a and combined with nine a and factor ten to build a fully colored, active intrinsic tenase complex. That complex pours out large amounts of factor ten a, shown by the bold white arrow feeding directly into the prothrombinase complex below, which is also fully assembled with factor five a, ten a, and prothrombin. The result is a massive, sustained wave of thrombin, factor two a, which in turn keeps reinforcing its own production by continuing to activate factors five and eight. This self-amplifying loop, running on the activated platelet surface, is what generates the huge thrombin burst responsible for building a stable, cross-linked fibrin clot.
keypoints: Extrinsic tenase fades out once TFPI has shut it down
Intrinsic tenase, factor eight a plus nine a, becomes the dominant ten a source
Prothrombinase, factor five a plus ten a, is now fully assembled
Sustained thrombin feedback drives the explosive propagation burst
keypoint_voiceover: By propagation, extrinsic tenase has faded out and intrinsic tenase takes over as the main ten a factory. With prothrombinase fully assembled and thrombin continuously reinforcing its own cofactors, you get the explosive thrombin burst that builds a stable clot.
